newsitem.title: USA: Northern Border rejects joint Iowa-Chicago pipe.
newsitem.headline: Northern Border rejects joint Iowa-Chicago pipe.

text.p: Natural Gas Pipeline Co of America said Tuesday that Northern Border Pipeline Co rejected a proposal for the two companies to merge their competing plans to build new pipeline capacity between Iowa and Chicago.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission late last year urged the two companies to construct a single pipeline or simply expand Natural's existing pipeline in order to limit environmental harm.
Both Natural's pipeline expansion and Northern Border's new pipeline to Chicago were designed to handle new natural gas deliveries from Canada on an expanded Northern Border system.
In comments filed on the commission's draft environmental review of the two plans, Natural said Northern Border turned down a proposal to use Natural's expansion.
"Northern Border declined Natural's offer on February 7, 1997 and made no counterproposal," Natural said.
Natural said it had proposed that Northern Border should not build its extension and instead contract for long-term transportation service on Natural's expanded pipeline.
In return, Northern Border would be able to use the capacity to provide service to all new shippers between Harper and Chicago, including those who had agreements with Natural.
Natural said that since Northern Border had rejected its offer, it was ready to go ahead with its pipeline extension, intended to ship an extra 663 million cubic feet a day of gas.
The FERC had said a single system, involving Northern Border's pipeline extension instead of Natural's expansion would have been preferable, but Natural said the commission was wrong.

Natural said expanding its pipeline with Northern Border onboard would be more practical because it made use of an existing pipeline corridor, it would cost $200 million less, would have lower rates with Northern Border's tariff, and would give new shippers access to all of Natural's delivery points.
Natural is a subsidiary of Occidental Petroleum Corp's MidCon Corp.

Officials at Northern Border, which is 70 percent owned by Enron Corp and 30 percent owned by TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, were not immediately available to comment on their filing to the FERC, which was due Tuesday.
